documentNotes.title: Instructions
documentNotes.statement:
1. Do not open the exam envelop yourself.
2. This part of the exam consists of 7\* problems located in separate exam stations.
3. You have 5 minutes to complete each problem.
4. After “out of time” is signaled, stop all actions and remain at the same station.
5. After “next station” is signaled, proceed to the next exam station and hand the exam envelope to the station’s proctor.
6. Use only blue pen to mark into the answer sheets provided. Any answers written in the answer sheet at the end of timer is considered final and will be graded towards the final score.

\* Number of problems will be reduced to 5 if night observation was successful

transcription.notes: Page 1 (instructions) is headed “Observational Examination (Day)”; pages 2–10 (the problem sheets) are headed “Observational Examination (Night)” as printed — kept as printed; the masthead of page 1 is used as the paper title. Page 1 footnote: the number of problems will be reduced to 5 if night observation was successful; all 7 printed problems are transcribed. No points are printed anywhere; points are null. No official solutions are in the archive, so no answers are given. Answer-sheet blank lines (underscores after “LST of the image:”, “Number of Planets visible:”, etc.) are omitted; the answer labels are kept. Printed forms kept verbatim: “envelop” in instruction 1 (a real word; “envelope” is used in instruction 5); agreement error kept as printed per D-P28: “Any answers written in the answer sheet at the end of timer is considered final” (plural subject with “is”). P7 prints the longitude as “10 ⁰ E” with a superscript zero used as a degree sign; kept as $10\ {}^{0}$ E. In the P1 table Rigil Kentaurus’s declination is printed with an en dash (–60°) while Antares and Spica use a minus sign (−); kept as printed. Page 4 has only the P3 answer line; page 5 is the full-page analemma graph; page 8 is the P5 data sheet (cropped as a figure). The student-code boxes and the IOAA logo are decoration.

problems.title: Analemma on another planet
problems.statement:
**Instruction:** Find the Obliquity (Axial Tilt) of the planet

**Included:**

- A generated analemma (position of a Star taken from the surface of a planet with interval separated by mean solar day of the planet over an orbital period around a Star) of a fictitious planet orbiting around a Star.
- Result is graphed on a paper with each major grid representing 5°

The obliquity of the planet :

problems.title: Find True North from Moon shadow
problems.statement:
**Instruction:** Draw an arrow pointing North in the data sheet

**Included:**

- Simulated position of moon shadows of a pole at certain intervals in the span of a day.
- The observer is located in the Southern hemisphere at latitude 27°S.
- The moon’s declination that night is +15°
- Ruler, Compass (drawing tool), Geometry kit

figures.alt: Photograph of a thin black vertical pole labelled “Pole” standing on a white surface, lit from the upper right; its long shadow runs to the lower left and ends on one of several small red cross marks on the ground.

figures.caption: Data sheet
figures.alt: Data sheet: a grey circle labelled “Pole” near the upper left and a series of small cross marks (shadow-tip positions) running diagonally from the upper left toward the lower right, the last one far to the right.

problems.statement:

**Included:**

- An Equatorial Mount Telescope that has already been **properly** aligned to a location in the northern celestial pole.
- Bubble Level.
- Latitude dial on the mount is covered (you may not use it).

problems.title: Precision Polar Alignment with Equatorial Mount
problems.statement:
**Instruction:** Perform a polar alignment on the equatorial mount provided

**Included:**

- Equatorial Mount with polar scope (has not been polar aligned)
- Date and Time (GMT, UTC+0) of the time performing the polar alignment
- Diagram of the sky’s position at the time
- A light source to be substituted with Polaris to be used for proper polar alignment (already visible in the polar scope)
- Longitude of observer
